entities.summary:
The first Battle of Mantinea fought in 418 BC during the Peloponnesian War was a pivotal clash between Sparta and its Peloponnesian allies against an allied force of Argos, Athens, and several others. This devastating defeat for the coalition marked a significant turning point in the war, as the Spartans successfully repelled the invading forces. The battle showcased the skill and tenacity of the Spartan warriors, who were able to utilize their unique phalanx formation to devastating effect, securing a crucial victory that would have far-reaching consequences for the Peloponnesian region.

The strategic genius of the Spartan commander, Brasidas, played a crucial role in the battle's outcome, as he cleverly employed the terrain to his advantage, funneling the enemy forces into a narrow killing zone. The bravery and martial prowess of the Spartan infantrymen, meanwhile, proved instrumental in securing the decisive victory.

The Battle of Mantinea's impact was felt long after the conflict had ended. The Spartan victory paved the way for the eventual defeat of Athens and its allies, marking the beginning of the end of the Peloponnesian War. The legacy of the battle can be seen in the continued dominance of Sparta in the region, as well as the enduring influence of the phalanx formation on the development of Western warfare.

The devastating losses suffered by the coalition forces at Mantinea were a stark reminder of the brutal realities of ancient warfare. 'The earth was wet with blood, and the groans of the dying were heard on all sides.' (Thucydides, The History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, Chapter 23)
